title: Maps: Representing the World on Paper
summary: How mapmakers turn the round Earth into flat, useful maps using projections, symbols, legends, scale, and different map types.
poll: A map does not need to be perfectly accurate to still be useful.

versions.title: What Is a Map?
versions.text:
What is a map? It is a flat picture of a place. You can hold it in your hands.

Earth is not flat. Earth is round like a ball. So how do you draw it on flat paper?

Map makers must stretch some parts. This is why shapes can look odd near the top.

A map needs marks. Small pictures stand for real things. A tiny tree might mean a forest.

These small pictures are called symbols. A map has a key. The key tells what each symbol means.

A map also has a scale. A scale shows how big real places are. One inch on the map may stand for many miles.

There are many kinds of maps. One kind shows countries. One kind shows hills and rivers. One kind shows roads for cars.

versions.title: Maps: Representing the World on Paper
versions.text:
What is a map? A map is a flat drawing that represents a real place, and you can hold one in your hands or view it on a screen.

Earth, however, is not flat at all. Earth is shaped like a sphere, so mapmakers face a real challenge when drawing a round planet onto flat paper.

Mapmakers must stretch certain parts of the world a little. This is why some shapes look a bit odd, especially near the top and bottom of many maps.

A map also needs clear marks to make sense to its reader. Small pictures, called symbols, stand in for real things on the ground, such as a tiny tree symbol standing for a whole forest.

Every good map includes a legend, sometimes called a key, which tells the reader exactly what each symbol on the map means.

A map likewise needs a scale, which tells the reader how a short distance on paper compares with a much longer distance in the real world.

Maps also come in several types. A political map shows countries and the borders between them. A physical map instead shows natural features, such as mountains and rivers. A road map focuses on highways and streets.

versions.title: Maps: Representing the World on Paper
versions.text:
What is a map? A map is a flat drawing that represents a real place, and a person can hold one in their hands or view it on a screen whenever it happens to be needed for some particular purpose.

Earth, however, is not flat at all; Earth is shaped like a sphere, so a cartographer, a person who designs maps professionally, faces a genuine and persistent challenge whenever attempting to render a round planet onto flat paper.

To solve this challenge, cartographers rely on a mathematical method called a projection, which converts the round surface of Earth into a flat image. Every projection introduces a certain amount of distortion, meaning that some shapes end up slightly stretched or squeezed, particularly near the top and bottom edges of the map, where the round surface curves away most sharply from the flat plane beneath it. No single projection can preserve shape, size, and distance all at once, so cartographers must choose whichever trade-off suits their particular purpose.

A map also requires clear marks to make sense to its reader. Small pictures, called symbols, stand in for real things on the ground, such as a tiny tree symbol that represents an entire forest or a small tent symbol that represents a campground somewhere nearby.

Every good map includes a legend, sometimes called a key, which tells the reader exactly what each symbol on the map actually represents, so that nobody is left guessing at its intended meaning.

A map likewise requires a scale, which tells the reader how a short distance measured on paper compares with a much longer distance in the real world, allowing anyone to estimate real distances fairly quickly and with reasonable accuracy.

Many maps are also marked with a grid of lines called latitude and longitude, which lets a reader pinpoint almost any exact location on Earth using only two simple numbers, a system that sailors and explorers have relied upon for centuries to navigate across open, featureless oceans.

Maps also come in several distinct types, each suited to a different purpose. A political map shows countries, states, and the borders drawn carefully between them. A physical map instead shows natural features, such as mountains and rivers, usually using color to indicate elevation clearly and precisely. A road map focuses specifically on the highways that drivers depend on every single day of their lives, often ignoring natural features almost entirely in favor of clarity.

Today, digital maps on phones and computers still rely on these same basic ideas, even though a satellite and a computer now handle the underlying projection automatically, instantly, and without any visible effort on the part of the user.

Earth, however, is not flat in the slightest; Earth is shaped like a sphere, so a cartographer, an individual who designs maps professionally, faces a genuine and persistent challenge whenever attempting to render a round planet onto flat paper.

To address this challenge, cartographers rely upon a mathematical method called a projection, which converts the round surface of Earth into a flat image. Every projection introduces a certain degree of distortion, meaning that some shapes end up slightly stretched or squeezed, particularly near the top and bottom edges of the map, where the round surface curves away most sharply from the flat plane beneath it. No single projection can simultaneously preserve shape, size, and distance, so cartographers must deliberately choose whichever trade-off best suits their particular purpose.

A map also requires clearly defined marks to make sense to its reader. Small pictures, called symbols, stand in for real things on the ground, such as a tiny tree symbol that represents an entire forest or a small tent symbol that represents a campground somewhere nearby.

Every well-made map includes a legend, sometimes called a key, which tells the reader precisely what each symbol on the map actually represents, so that nobody is left guessing at its intended meaning.

A map likewise requires a scale, which tells the reader how a short distance measured on paper compares with a much longer distance in the real world, allowing anyone to estimate real distances fairly quickly and with reasonable accuracy.

Many maps are also marked with a grid of lines called latitude and longitude, which lets a reader pinpoint almost any exact location on Earth using only two simple numbers, a system that sailors and explorers have relied upon for centuries to navigate across open, otherwise featureless oceans.

Maps also come in several distinct types, each one suited to a somewhat different purpose. A political map shows countries, states, and the borders drawn carefully between them, often in contrasting colors. A physical map instead shows natural features, such as mountains, deserts, and rivers, typically using color to indicate elevation clearly and precisely. A road map focuses specifically on the highways and streets that drivers depend on every single day of their lives, often ignoring natural features almost entirely in favor of absolute clarity.

Today, digital maps displayed on phones and computers still rely fundamentally on these same underlying ideas, even though a constellation of satellites and a powerful computer now handle the underlying projection automatically, instantly, and without any visible effort whatsoever on the part of the user, who simply expects the correct location to appear within a fraction of a second.

versions.title: Maps: Representing the World on Paper
versions.text:
What exactly is a map? A map is a flat representation that depicts a real place, and a person can hold one physically in their hands or view it digitally on a screen whenever it happens to be needed for some particular purpose, however mundane or significant that purpose might be.

Earth, however, is not flat in the slightest; Earth is shaped like a sphere, so a cartographer, an individual who designs maps professionally, faces a genuine and persistent challenge whenever attempting to render a thoroughly round planet onto perfectly flat paper.

To address this longstanding challenge, cartographers rely upon a mathematical method called a projection, which converts the round surface of Earth into a flat image through careful calculation. Every projection introduces a certain degree of distortion, meaning that some shapes end up slightly stretched or squeezed, particularly near the top and bottom edges of the map, where the round surface curves away most sharply from the flat plane beneath it. No single projection can simultaneously preserve shape, size, and distance with perfect fidelity, so cartographers must deliberately choose whichever trade-off best suits their particular purpose at hand.

A map also requires clearly defined marks to make sense to its reader. Small pictures, called symbols, stand in for real things on the ground, such as a tiny tree symbol that represents an entire forest or a small tent symbol that represents a campground situated somewhere nearby.

Every well-made map includes a legend, sometimes called a key, which tells the reader precisely what each symbol on the map actually represents, so that nobody is ever left guessing at its intended meaning.

A map likewise requires a scale, which tells the reader how a short distance measured on paper compares with a considerably longer distance in the real world, allowing anyone to estimate real distances fairly quickly and with reasonable accuracy, even without any specialized tools.

Many maps are also marked with a grid of lines called latitude and longitude, which lets a reader pinpoint almost any exact location on Earth using only two simple numbers, a system that sailors and explorers have relied upon for centuries in order to navigate across open, otherwise featureless oceans.

Maps also come in several distinct types, each one suited to a somewhat different purpose. A political map shows countries, states, and the borders drawn carefully between them, often rendered in contrasting colors for clarity. A physical map instead shows natural features, such as mountains, deserts, and rivers, typically using color to indicate elevation clearly and precisely. A road map focuses specifically on the highways and streets that drivers depend on every single day of their lives, often ignoring natural features almost entirely in favor of absolute clarity.

Today, digital maps displayed on phones and computers still rely fundamentally on these same underlying ideas, even though a constellation of orbiting satellites and a powerful computer now handle the underlying projection automatically, instantly, and without any visible effort whatsoever on the part of the user, who simply expects the correct location to appear within a fraction of a second, rarely pausing to consider the centuries of mathematical refinement that made such instant accuracy possible.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: Modern satellites have completely eliminated the need for map projections, so cartographers do not make any trade-offs now, since every map is perfect and shows no distortion at all, ever.
Every cartographer throughout history has used the exact same single projection, so maps from every country, every century, and every culture look alike and never change at all.

Cartographers must make deliberate trade-offs when turning Earth's round surface into a flat map, using tools like projections, symbols, legends, scale, and coordinate grids despite unavoidable distortion.
Latitude and longitude were invented only after digital maps already existed, so earlier sailors and travelers had no way to describe any place on Earth at all, even with a compass and a chart.
questions.why: The article's main point is that cartographers balance several tools and trade-offs to make useful, if imperfect, flat maps.

wrong.A: Satellites still rely on projection math; they have not removed the need for it.
wrong.B: The article describes different projections, not one single universal choice.
wrong.D: Latitude and longitude long predate digital maps.

questions.stem: According to the article, why can no single projection be perfect?
